mainTopic: Defending רב יהודה on conditional נדרים, how a vow can forbid marital relations, and the start of a new משנה on oaths and phrasings with קרבן.
overview: רב יהודה holds that if a נדר depends on a later condition, a person may not do the forbidden act now, because it might turn into a broken נדר after the fact. The גמרא tests this against several sources. It defends him each time. Some sources only describe what happens after the fact ('if she benefited,' 'he ate'), not what is allowed from the start. רבא explains that even before the wife goes to her father's house she is forbidden, and going only adds lashes. In the loaf ברייתא, the wording 'he went' was chosen only to match 'he ate,' so it proves nothing. The גמרא then asks how a husband can vow against relations with his wife when the Torah obligates him. It answers that he forbids his own pleasure, not his duty, and רב כהנא's ruling about a wife's vow supports this. Finally a new משנה begins. A שבועה not to sleep, speak, or walk is binding, but certain phrasings using the word קרבן leave the food permitted.

steps.title: The challenge is declared a full refutation of רב יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its previous challenge by declaring it a decisive refutation of רב יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is a full refutation of רב יהודה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא just showed that the משנה seems to let the wife benefit before the condition happens. Now it says this completely knocks down רב יהודה's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה said you may not do something now that could later become a broken נדר. The inference from the משנה ('she went, forbidden; didn't go, permitted') suggests she may benefit now. So the גמרא calls it a תיובתא, the strongest kind of challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא whose rule about conditional נדרים is being challenged

phrases.english: And this is a refutation of Rav Yehuda!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenge raised just before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's rule that one may not do now an act that could later become a broken נדר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה seems to permit benefit before the condition is met, which goes against רב יהודה.

steps.title: The משנה only describes the result after the fact
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reinterprets the משנה: it is not permitting benefit from the start. It is saying that if she benefited and then the condition happened, she broke בל יחל דברו.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the משנה teaches this, it means that if she did benefit, she is in violation of 'He shall not break his word.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב יהודה. It explains that the משנה is describing what happens if she already benefited, not what she is allowed to do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge read the משנה as לכתחילה permission. The answer reads it as a בדיעבד statement: once the condition is met, her earlier benefit counts as breaking the נדר. This fits רב יהודה's view perfectly.

keyTerms.meaning: When it teaches, meaning this is what the source really means
He shall not break his word, the prohibition against breaking a נדר
After the fact, as opposed to permission from the start

steps.confusionAlert: The משנה's words are not saying 'she is allowed to benefit before she goes.' According to this answer, they describe what happens if she already did benefit.

phrases.english: When it teaches, it means that if she benefited,
she is in violation of "He shall not break his word."

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָתָנֵי, דְּאִי אִיתְהֲנִי הֲרֵי זֶה בְּבַל יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the source: a בדיעבד description, not לכתחילה permission
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה permits her to benefit before the condition happens.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה only says that benefit already taken becomes a violation once the condition is met. רב יהודה stands.

steps.title: A second משנה: benefit forbidden until סוכות if she goes before פסח
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes another משנה. A husband forbids his wife to benefit from him until סוכות if she goes to her father's house before פסח.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: 'Benefit from me until סוכות is forbidden to you if you go to your father's house before פסח.' If she went before פסח, she may not benefit from him until סוכות, and she may go to her father's house after פסח.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a new משנה to set up a fresh challenge against רב יהודה. The challenge itself comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The condition (going to her father's house) only counts until פסח, so going after פסח is fine. If she went before פסח, the נדר takes effect and she may not benefit until סוכות. The exact wording of this משנה will be used for a new inference.

keyTerms.meaning: She is forbidden to benefit from him

phrases.english: We learned: "[Forbidden is] what you benefit from me until the festival
phrases.notes: The word קונם (forbidden) is understood here. The festival means סוכות.

phrases.aramaic: אִם תֵּלְכִי לְבֵית אָבִיךְ עַד הַפֶּסַח״,
phrases.english: if you go to your father's house until Passover,"
if she went before Passover,
she is forbidden to benefit from him until the festival,
and she is permitted to go after Passover.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: שֶׁאַתְּ נֶהֱנֵית לִי עַד הֶחָג אִם תֵּלְכִי לְבֵית אָבִיךְ עַד הַפֶּסַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רב יהודה, the גמרא brings a new source to test him again.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Going before פסח triggers a ban on benefit until סוכות. Going after פסח is permitted.

steps.title: The inference: if she did not go, benefit is allowed
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's wording, the גמרא infers that only if she went is she forbidden. If she did not go, she may benefit now. This seems to go against רב יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she went, she is forbidden. If she did not go, she is not forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the משנה closely. It suggests the wife may benefit now, before she knows whether she will go, which challenges רב יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה would say she must not benefit now, because if she goes before פסח her benefit becomes a broken נדר. The משנה's wording implies that as long as she hasn't gone, there is no ban. That looks like permission to benefit now.

keyTerms.meaning: An inference drawn from the exact wording of a source

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a second test of רב יהודה's rule. רבא answers it in the next step.

phrases.english: She went, she is forbidden;
she did not go, she is not.
phrases.notes: The גמרא reads this as letting her benefit now, even though she might still go before פסח.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the challenging inference from the משנה quoted in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's rule that one may not do now an act that could later become a broken נדר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's wording implies she may benefit while she has not yet gone, even though she might go before פסח and make that benefit a violation.

steps.title: רבא: She is forbidden even before she goes
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers the challenge from the משנה. Even if she did not go, she is forbidden. Going only adds lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Really, even if she did not go, she is forbidden. If she went, she is forbidden and gets lashes. If she did not go, she is just forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends רב יהודה. He says the משנה does not mean she may benefit before going. It only means that once she has gone, benefiting from him makes her liable to lashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge in step 4 read the משנה as 'only if she went is she forbidden.' רבא changes what 'forbidden' means there. Before going she is already forbidden, but only as a precaution with no lashes. After going, the vow fully takes effect and she gets lashes. So the משנה fits רב יהודה.

phrases.english: Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ לֹא הָלְכָה אֲסוּרָה.
phrases.english: The same is true, that even if she did not go, she is forbidden.
If she went, she is forbidden and is flogged;
if she did not go, she is merely forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ לֹא הָלְכָה אֲסוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 against רב יהודה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: the משנה is distinguishing between a plain prohibition and lashes, not between forbidden and permitted.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה implies that if she has not gone yet, she may benefit now.
steps.terutzMaskana: She is forbidden either way. Going only adds lashes.

steps.title: Challenge from the loaf ברייתא: he ate it today
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא about a loaf forbidden today if he goes somewhere tomorrow seems to allow eating it today.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: 'This loaf is forbidden to me today if I go to such-and-such place tomorrow.' If he ate it, he is now under 'he shall not go'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge רב יהודה. It seems to show that a person may eat the loaf before the condition is decided.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The condition (going tomorrow) is decided only after the eating (today). The ברייתא seems calm about him eating today and just tells him not to go tomorrow. That suggests eating before the condition is decided is allowed, which goes against רב יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: they raised an objection (from a ברייתא or משנה)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
"This loaf is forbidden to me today
if I go to such-and-such a place tomorrow";
if he ate it, he is under "he shall not go"!
phrases.notes: Once he has eaten it, going tomorrow would make that eating forbidden after the fact. So now he may not go.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: כִּכָּר זוֹ עָלַי הַיּוֹם אִם אֵלֵךְ לְמָקוֹם פְּלוֹנִי לְמָחָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבא's defense, a new source is brought against רב יהודה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's view that one may not benefit before the condition is decided.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא seems to allow eating today, before it is known whether he will go tomorrow.

steps.title: 'He ate' means after the fact, not permission
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says 'he ate,' not 'he may eat.' It only describes what happens if he already ate.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does it say 'he may eat'? It says 'he ate.' It means: once he has eaten, he is under 'he shall not go.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by looking closely at the exact word in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אוכל' would mean he is allowed to eat from the start. 'אכל' only describes something already done. So the ברייתא teaches what happens after he ate, and does not say eating is allowed. רב יהודה is safe.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch the tense. אוכל (present: 'eats, may eat') is permission from the start. אכל (past: 'ate') only describes what already happened.

phrases.english: Does it teach "he may eat"?
It teaches "he ate":

phrases.aramaic: דְּכִי אֲכַל הֲרֵי זֶה בְּ״בַל יֵלֵךְ״.
phrases.english: that once he ate, he is under "he shall not go."

steps.terutzResolutionType: Precise reading of the wording (past tense, after the fact).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא allows eating the loaf today.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only tells us the result if he already ate. It gives no permission to eat.

steps.title: Later in the ברייתא: going is the forbidden act, so a difficulty for רב יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if he went, he broke his word. So going is what is forbidden, which suggests eating was allowed. This is difficult for רב יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he went, he breaks 'he shall not profane his word.' Going from the start is not allowed. This is difficult for רב יהודה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the next line of the same ברייתא. It finds a new problem for רב יהודה that the earlier answer does not solve.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא treats going as the act a person must avoid from the start. That suggests the eating before it was allowed, and only afterwards does going become forbidden. This fits רב נחמן, who allows making a vow take effect, and goes against רב יהודה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This second line of the ברייתא seems to back רב נחמן's view that a person may act now and let the conditional vow take effect later. The next step shows how רב יהודה reads the wording so that it does not disprove him.

phrases.aramaic: הָלַךְ — הֲרֵי זֶה בְּ״בַל יַחֵל״ דְּבָרוֹ.
phrases.english: If he went, he is in violation of "he shall not profane his word."
Going from the start: no.
And this is difficult for Rav Yehuda!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָלַךְ הֲרֵי זֶה בְּבַל יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first line of the ברייתא was answered, the next line is used to renew the challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's view that one may not benefit before the condition is decided.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא forbids going from the start, so going is the act to avoid. This implies the eating before it was allowed.

steps.title: The ברייתא said 'he went' only to match 'he ate'
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that the ברייתא could have said 'he may go.' It wrote 'he went' only to keep the same past-tense style as its first part, 'he ate.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה could answer you: the ברייתא really could have said 'he may go.' But its first part said 'he ate,' because it could not say 'he may eat.' So the second part also said 'he went,' to match.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last challenge against רב יהודה from step 8. It explains that the wording 'he went' does not prove that eating was allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that 'if he went' means going was the forbidden act and eating was fine. רב יהודה says the first part had to say 'he ate,' because eating is not allowed at the start. The second part simply copied that past-tense style. So the wording tells us nothing about what is allowed, and רב יהודה's view stands.

keyTerms.meaning: the same is true; it could just as well have said
since it teaches; used when one wording is chosen to match another
the first part of a teaching
the last part of a teaching

steps.whatToRemember: Sometimes a ברייתא picks its wording only to match its other clause. When that happens, you cannot draw a legal inference from that word, so רב יהודה is not disproven.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda could say to you:
the same is true, it could have taught "he may go."
But since the first part teaches "he ate,"
phrases.notes: This is the loaf case from step 6: he is forbidden to eat the loaf today if he goes to a certain place tomorrow.

phrases.english: since it cannot teach "he may eat"
phrases.notes: In רב יהודה's view, eating is not allowed at the start, so the ברייתא could only describe it after the fact.

phrases.english: the last part also teaches "he went."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8 by explaining the ברייתא's wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Stylistic parallelism: the wording follows the earlier clause and carries no legal weight.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'If he went, he broke his word' suggests that only going was forbidden, so eating must have been allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא said 'he went' only to match 'he ate.' It could just as well have said 'he may go,' so רב יהודה is not disproven.

steps.title: The משנה's case of a husband's vow against relations
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: a husband who says 'Relations with you are קונם' is bound by בל יחל דברו.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man who says to his wife, 'It is קונם that I have relations with you,' is under the law of 'He shall not break his word.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. It is setting up a question about how this vow can work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats this vow as binding, so breaking it would violate בל יחל דברו. This quote prepares the next step, where the גמרא asks how a man can forbid something the Torah obligates him to give.

keyTerms.meaning: a word used to make something forbidden by a vow, like a קרבן
'he shall not break his word': the Torah's ban on breaking a vow

phrases.english: One who says to his wife
"It is konam that I have relations with you,"
is subject to "He shall not break his word."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the רב יהודה discussion to a new clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A husband's vow forbidding relations with his wife takes effect, and breaking it violates בל יחל דברו.

steps.title: But the Torah obligates him to his wife
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how this vow can work. The Torah already obligates the husband to give his wife marital relations (עונה).
steps.simpleTranslation: But he is bound to her by Torah law, as it says: 'Her food, her clothing, and her conjugal rights he shall not reduce!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה. A person cannot use a vow to get out of a duty he already owes by Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow can forbid things that belong to the person making it. It cannot cancel what he owes someone else. Since the husband owes his wife עונה from the Torah, it seems his vow against relations should not take effect at all.

keyTerms.meaning: is obligated or bound to someone

phrases.english: But he is obligated to her by Torah law,
as it is written:
"Her food, her clothing, and her conjugal rights he shall not reduce!"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה quoted in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a husband's vow against relations takes effect.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A vow cannot cancel a Torah obligation owed to another person, and the husband owes his wife עונה by Torah law.

steps.title: He vowed against his own pleasure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about a husband who says, 'The pleasure of relations with you is forbidden to me.' Here he forbids his own pleasure, not his duty to her.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is when he says, 'The pleasure of relations with you is forbidden to me,' and so he does not want relations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the vow can work. It is worded about the husband's own pleasure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow saying 'I will not have relations with you' tries to cancel his duty, so it fails. But his own pleasure is his to forbid, and he owes it to no one. So a vow on his pleasure does take effect, and relations become forbidden as a result.

keyTerms.meaning: the pleasure of relations with you is forbidden to me
it is pleasing or wanted by him

steps.confusionAlert: The vow does not cancel the wife's rights head-on. It works only because it targets his own pleasure. Forbidding the act itself would not take effect.

phrases.english: When he says, "The pleasure of relations with you is forbidden to me,"

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא לָא קָא נִיחָא לֵיהּ בְּתַשְׁמִישׁ.
phrases.english: and so relations are not wanted by him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11 by narrowing the case of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the vow is worded about his own pleasure, not about the act he owes her.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The vow forbids relations directly, which would go against his Torah obligation.
steps.terutzMaskana: The vow forbids his own pleasure, which he may forbid, so it takes effect.

steps.title: רב כהנא shows the difference between the act and the pleasure
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא rules on a wife's vow. If she forbids relations to him, she is forced to keep her duty. If she forbids her own pleasure, relations are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב כהנא said: if she says 'Relations with me are forbidden to you,' we force her and she has relations with him, because she is obligated to him. If she says 'The pleasure of relations with you is forbidden to me,' relations are forbidden, because we do not feed a person something forbidden to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב כהנא as support for the answer in step 12. A vow about one's own pleasure works, even though a vow against a duty does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case, the wife tries to take away what she owes her husband, so the vow does not work and she is forced to keep her duty. In the second case, she forbids her own pleasure. That vow works, and since we may not make anyone take something forbidden to them, relations are forbidden. This is exactly the difference the גמרא used to explain the husband's vow.

keyTerms.meaning: we force her; the court compels her

keyTerms.term: אֵין מַאֲכִילִין לוֹ לְאָדָם דָּבָר הָאָסוּר לוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: we do not feed a person something forbidden to him

steps.whatToRemember: A vow cannot cancel what you owe someone else ('my relations are forbidden to you'). But you can forbid your own pleasure ('the pleasure is forbidden to me'), and then the act becomes forbidden as a result.
steps.whyThisMatters: This idea, that you can forbid your own pleasure but not cancel a duty, explains how vows can affect marital obligations at all.

phrases.english: As Rav Kahana said:
If a wife says, "Relations with me are forbidden to you,"
we force her, and she has relations with him,
because she is obligated to him.
If she says, "The pleasure of relations with you is forbidden to me,"
relations are forbidden,
because we do not feed a person
something that is forbidden to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 12 with a parallel ruling about a wife's vow.
steps.raayaObject: The difference between forbidding the act owed to a spouse and forbidding one's own pleasure from it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב כהנא's ruling: 'תשמישי עליך' does not take effect and she is forced, while 'הנאת תשמישך עלי' takes effect and relations are forbidden.

steps.title: An oath not to sleep, speak, or walk is binding
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if a person swears with a שבועה that he will not sleep, speak, or walk, the action is אסור to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone says, 'I swear that I will not sleep,' or 'that I will not speak,' or 'that I will not walk,' he is forbidden to do it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new משנה. It teaches that a שבועה can forbid a person from doing an action, such as sleeping, speaking, or walking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the daf discussed vows of קונם, which forbid an object, such as relations described as a source of pleasure. Here the משנה uses a שבועה, which binds the person himself. That is why it can work even on an action like sleeping, which is not an object at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה. It marks the start of a new משנה.
An oath. It binds the person to do or not do something.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the קונם vows earlier on the daf. Those forbid an object. This is a שבועה, which binds the person to an action.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
An oath that I will not sleep,
that I will not speak,
that I will not walk,
it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: He means the action he swore about is now forbidden to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the discussion of קונם on marital relations in steps 10 to 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שבועה not to sleep, speak, or walk is binding. The action becomes אסור.

steps.title: Three phrasings with the word 'offering' that do not work
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists three phrasings that use the word קרבן: 'קרבן, I will not eat of yours,' 'הא קרבן that I will eat of yours,' and 'לא קרבן, I will not eat of yours.' In all three cases the food stays מותר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says, 'An offering, I will not eat of yours,' or 'הא קרבן that I will eat of yours,' or 'Not an offering, I will not eat of yours,' the food is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with three ways of speaking that mention a קרבן. It rules that none of them forbids the food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A normal vow works by making food 'like a קרבן' for the person. In these three phrasings the word קרבן appears, but the sentence does not clearly make the food like an offering, so no איסור takes effect. The משנה does not explain each phrase, which sets up the גמרא's discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: An offering. This is the standard word used to make a vow on food.
A phrasing with הא. It can be read as 'this offering' or 'behold, an offering.'
'Not an offering.' The phrasing denies that the food is a קרבן.
Permitted. The vow does not take effect.

steps.whatToRemember: A שבועה can forbid actions like sleeping. However, just saying the word קרבן does not make a vow. These three phrasings leave the food מותר.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume that any sentence with the word קרבן in it creates a vow. The משנה is teaching exactly the opposite here.

phrases.english: An offering, I will not eat of yours,
'Ha korban' that I will eat of yours,
phrases.notes: The word הָא is unclear here. It may mean 'this' or 'behold.' The גמרא will discuss what it means.

phrases.english: Not an offering, I will not eat of yours,
it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה, moving from oaths on actions to phrasings with קרבן that fail to create a vow.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The phrasings 'קרבן, I will not eat of yours,' 'הא קרבן that I will eat of yours,' and 'לא קרבן, I will not eat of yours' do not create a vow. The food is מותר.
